📖 Worked example — from anonymous class to lambda

WORKED EXAMPLE — the same behavior, three shrinking forms
// 1. Anonymous class (the old way)
Comparator<String> byLen = new Comparator<String>() {
    public int compare(String a, String b) {
        return a.length() - b.length();
    }
};
// 2. Lambda — parameters -> expression
Comparator<String> byLen2 = (a, b) -> a.length() - b.length();
// 3. Used:
list.sort(byLen2);        // shortest strings first
A lambda IS an implementation of a one-method interface, minus the ceremony. (a, b) are the method’s parameters; the expression is its return value. Types are inferred from the target interface.
⚠️ ONE ABSTRACT METHOD REQUIRED
Lambdas only work where the target type is a functional interface (exactly one abstract method). Two abstract methods → no lambda possible — the compiler error, not a style choice.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Lambda expressions are the syntactic gateway to functional programming in Java. Once you internalize them, half the boilerplate of pre-Java-8 code disappears and the Streams API becomes natural. They are the single biggest leap from 'Java the verbose' to 'Java the modern.'

Core concepts

1. What a lambda actually is. A lambda expression is an unnamed function — parameters, an arrow, and a body. (a, b) -> a + b is the entire definition. Java compiles it to an instance of a functional interface (one whose only abstract method matches the signature). The lambda IS an object; it just looks like an expression.

2. Syntax forms. (int a, int b) -> a + b — fully explicit. (a, b) -> a + b — types inferred. x -> x * 2 — single parameter, no parens. () -> 42 — no parameters. (a, b) -> { return a + b; } — block body with explicit return. Pick the shortest form that reads clearly.

3. Effectively final captures. A lambda can use local variables from its enclosing scope only if they are 'effectively final' — never reassigned after initialization. The compiler enforces this. The reason: lambdas may outlive the stack frame that created them, so mutating captured variables would be unsafe.

4. Lambdas vs anonymous classes. Before lambdas, you wrote new Comparator<String() { public int compare(String a, String b) { return a.length() - b.length(); } }. With lambdas: (a, b) -> a.length() - b.length(). Same bytecode-level behavior in most cases, dramatically less code. Anonymous classes still exist for multi-method interfaces.

5. Method references — the shorter cousin. When a lambda just calls a single method, replace it with a method reference. s -> s.toUpperCase() becomes String::toUpperCase. (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a, b) becomes Integer::compare. Reads better and shows intent — covered in detail in section 3.

6. Where lambdas thrive. Anywhere an interface has a single abstract method: Runnable, Comparator, Predicate, Function, event listeners, Stream operations. The Java standard library is heavily lambda-friendly post-Java-8; using lambdas there is now the idiomatic style.

7. Lambdas have limits. They cannot replace classes that need multiple methods, instance state, or constructors. A lambda is a one-method object. When you need more, anonymous class or full class is still right. Don't force-fit.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Trying to mutate a captured local variable — compile error and refactoring to use an array or AtomicInteger is rarely the right answer; redesign instead.
  • Overusing lambdas for code that should be a named method — long inline lambdas hurt readability.
  • Forgetting that 'this' inside a lambda refers to the enclosing class, NOT to the lambda itself (unlike anonymous classes).
  • Treating lambdas as a pure-style replacement for everything — sometimes a regular for loop is clearer.

Quick recap

A lambda is an unnamed function compiled to an instance of a functional interface. Syntax forms range from terse (single param) to block-bodied. Captured locals must be effectively final. Lambdas replace most anonymous-class boilerplate. Method references shorten them further when applicable.

Glossary

Lambda expression
An unnamed function: parameters, arrow, body.
Functional interface
Interface with exactly one abstract method; lambdas are compiled into these.
Effectively final
A local variable that is never reassigned after initialization, even without the final keyword.
Anonymous class
Pre-Java-8 way to provide a single-use instance of an interface; mostly replaced by lambdas.
Method reference
Compact form replacing a lambda that just delegates to one method (Class::method or instance::method).

📖 Worked example — the four core functional interfaces

WORKED EXAMPLE — one of each, doing real work
Predicate<String>  isLong  = s -> s.length() > 5;   // test:  T → boolean
Function<String,Integer> len = s -> s.length();      // apply: T → R
Consumer<String>   print   = s -> System.out.println(s); // accept: T → void
Supplier<String>   make    = () -> "hello";          // get:   () → T

isLong.test("banana");   // true
len.apply("cat");        // 3
print.accept("hi");      // prints hi
make.get();              // "hello"
Memory hook by shape: Predicate judges, Function transforms, Consumer uses up, Supplier produces. Streams are built on exactly these four — filter takes a Predicate, map takes a Function, forEach takes a Consumer.
⚠️ MATCH THE SHAPE, NOT THE NAME
Exam questions describe a lambda and ask its interface: look at what goes IN and what comes OUT. () → value is Supplier; value → boolean is Predicate; value → value is Function; value → nothing is Consumer.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Lambdas are typed as functional interfaces. The java.util.function package provides ~40 of them covering nearly every common shape. Knowing the standard four (Function, Predicate, Consumer, Supplier) plus their variants stops you from inventing custom interfaces unnecessarily.

Core concepts

1. The functional interface contract. Exactly one abstract method (a Single Abstract Method, SAM). Default and static methods don't count. The annotation @FunctionalInterface enforces this at compile time and documents intent. Apply it to any interface you intend lambdas to target.

2. Function<T, R. Takes a T, returns an R. The shape of any transformation: String::length is Function<String, Integer. Compose with andThen and compose. Most Stream.map calls take a Function.

3. Predicate<T. Takes a T, returns boolean. The shape of any test or filter. s -> s.isBlank() is Predicate<String. Combine with and, or, negate. The bedrock of Stream.filter.

4. Consumer<T. Takes a T, returns nothing. Side-effect interface: logging, printing, mutating. Stream.forEach takes a Consumer. Chain with andThen for sequenced consumers.

5. Supplier<T. Takes nothing, returns a T. Used for lazy or factory-style creation: Optional.orElseGet(Supplier), Stream.generate(Supplier). Defers work until needed.

6. Specialized primitive variants. Boxing primitives in Function<Integer, ... wastes time. IntFunction, ToIntFunction, IntPredicate, IntConsumer, IntSupplier (and Long/Double versions) skip the boxing. Use them in performance-sensitive code, especially inside Streams.

7. BiFunction, BiPredicate, BiConsumer. Two-argument variants. (a, b) -> a + b can fit a BinaryOperator<Integer (which extends BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer). Beyond two arguments, define your own functional interface — three-arg variants aren't in the standard library.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Reinventing functional interfaces when java.util.function already has one with the right shape.
  • Boxing primitives in performance-critical code — use IntFunction etc.
  • Adding multiple abstract methods and being surprised that lambdas no longer fit.
  • Misreading Function<T, R generics — T is the input, R the result; right-to-left in the signature.

Quick recap

A functional interface has exactly one abstract method. The big four are Function, Predicate, Consumer, Supplier. Use Bi-variants for two-argument shapes. Use Int/Long/Double specializations to avoid boxing. @FunctionalInterface documents and enforces the contract.

Glossary

Functional interface
Interface with one abstract method; targetable by lambdas and method references.
@FunctionalInterface
Annotation enforcing the SAM rule at compile time.
Function<T, R
T -> R; the basic transformation.
Predicate<T
T -> boolean; the basic test.
Consumer<T
T -> void; the basic side-effect.

📖 Worked example — method references, all four kinds

WORKED EXAMPLE — lambda ↔ reference, side by side
s -> s.toUpperCase()          ⇔   String::toUpperCase   // instance method,
                                                        // via the parameter
s -> System.out.println(s)    ⇔   System.out::println   // instance method,
                                                        // on a specific object
s -> Integer.parseInt(s)      ⇔   Integer::parseInt     // static method
() -> new ArrayList<>()       ⇔   ArrayList::new        // constructor

names.stream().map(String::toUpperCase).forEach(System.out::println);
A method reference is a lambda whose body ONLY calls an existing method with the same arguments, in the same order. If the lambda does anything extra (adds 1, flips arguments), it cannot become a reference.
⚠️ String::toUpperCase HAS A HIDDEN PARAMETER
ClassName::instanceMethod means “call it ON the first lambda parameter” — s.toUpperCase(). That’s different from object::method, where the receiver is fixed. Distinguishing those two forms is the exam’s favorite.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Method references are not just syntactic sugar — they signal intent. List.forEach(System.out::println) reads as 'print each.' List.forEach(x -> System.out.println(x)) reads as 'for each, take x and call println.' Same behavior; the reference form is shorter and more obvious.

Core concepts

1. Static method reference. ClassName::staticMethod. Integer::parseInt replaces s -> Integer.parseInt(s). Math::max replaces (a, b) -> Math.max(a, b). Most utility methods on standard classes are reachable this way.

2. Bound instance method reference. instance::method. Captures a specific receiver. logger::info — lambda becomes msg -> logger.info(msg). The instance is part of the reference.

3. Unbound instance method reference. ClassName::instanceMethod. The receiver is supplied at call time. String::toUpperCase — a Function<String, String where the input becomes the receiver. Common in Stream.map for instance methods.

4. Constructor reference. ClassName::new. ArrayList::new is a Supplier<ArrayList (or an IntFunction<ArrayList if you want sized creation). Used in Stream.collect, Optional, factories.

5. Method references vs lambdas — when which. If the lambda body is just a call passing arguments straight through, prefer the reference. If you need to reorder arguments, transform values, or add logic, use a lambda. Don't contort code to fit a reference.

6. Type inference and overload disambiguation. Method references rely on the target functional interface to disambiguate overloads. Integer::parseInt has two overloads; the compiler picks based on context. When ambiguous, fall back to a lambda or use an explicit cast.

7. Refactoring lambdas to references. Modern IDEs suggest the conversion. Accept it when the result reads clearly. Reject it when the lambda's intent is non-obvious from the reference alone (rare, but real).

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Converting a lambda to a reference where the new form is harder to read — readability beats brevity.
  • Confusing bound and unbound forms — String::length vs str::length differ in what they capture.
  • Using ClassName::new when a static factory method would document intent better.
  • Trusting auto-conversion blindly — sometimes the IDE suggests a reference that breaks overload resolution at runtime.

Quick recap

Method references replace single-call lambdas with a more declarative form: Class::staticMethod, instance::method, Class::instanceMethod, Class::new. Each has its niche. Use them when they read better, not because they are shorter. The compiler resolves which functional interface they target based on context.

Glossary

Method reference
Compact lambda form: Class::method or instance::method.
Static method reference
ClassName::staticMethod, lambda becomes args -> ClassName.staticMethod(args).
Bound instance method reference
instance::method — the receiver is captured.
Unbound instance method reference
ClassName::instanceMethod — the receiver becomes the first argument.
Constructor reference
ClassName::new — used as a Supplier or factory.

Method references are lambdas in shorthand: String::valueOf is exactly equivalent to x -> String.valueOf(x). And Comparator.comparing(Person::getAge) builds a comparator that orders by the extracted key — the age — no manual compareTo needed.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The Streams API is where lambdas pay back the most. Filter, map, reduce, collect — operations that took 10 lines of imperative code become single, readable expressions. But streams have specific semantics (lazy, single-use, source-bound) that bite if you misunderstand them.

Core concepts

1. A stream is not a collection. It is a sequence of elements with a pipeline of operations attached. Streams don't store data; they describe computation. list.stream() doesn't copy the list — it creates a view onto it.

2. Three-part pipeline. Source (collection, array, generator) → zero or more intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted) → exactly one terminal operation (collect, forEach, count). The terminal triggers execution; without it, nothing runs.

3. Lazy evaluation. Intermediate operations are recorded but not executed until a terminal operation runs. This lets the runtime fuse operations and short-circuit. stream.filter(pred).findFirst() may stop at the first match without scanning the rest.

4. Single-use. Once a terminal operation runs, the stream is consumed. Trying to use it again throws IllegalStateException. If you need to reuse, recreate from the source. This is unlike collections, which are reusable.

5. Creating streams. Collection.stream() — most common. Stream.of(a, b, c) — fixed elements. IntStream.range(0, 100) — primitive range. Files.lines(path) — file as stream. Stream.generate(supplier) and Stream.iterate(seed, fn) — infinite streams (always pair with limit).

6. Order matters in pipelines. filter then sorted is cheaper than sorted then filter — sorting fewer elements is faster. The compiler doesn't reorder for you; arrange operations to maximize early elimination.

7. Streams vs imperative loops. Streams shine for transformations, multi-step processing, parallel work, and declarative readability. Loops still win for: complex multi-variable state, early break with side effects, single-pass operations on small data. Match tool to task.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Reusing a stream after a terminal — IllegalStateException.
  • Forgetting the terminal operation — the pipeline silently does nothing.
  • Modifying the source collection mid-stream — undefined behavior.
  • Heavy side effects inside intermediate operations — defeats laziness and parallelism guarantees.

Quick recap

A stream pipeline has a source, intermediate ops, and one terminal. Operations are lazy; terminals trigger. Streams are single-use. Order operations to filter early. Use streams for transformations and multi-step processing; stick with loops when state and short-circuiting need direct control.

Glossary

Stream
A sequence of elements with a pipeline of operations; not a data store.
Source
The origin of stream elements (collection, array, file, generator).
Intermediate operation
Returns a stream; lazy; e.g., filter, map, sorted.
Terminal operation
Triggers pipeline execution; produces a result or side effect.
Lazy evaluation
Operations execute only when a terminal demands a result.
"},"D387/ch2/s2":{"body":"

📖 Worked example — chaining intermediate operations

WORKED EXAMPLE — filter → map → sorted, traced
List<String> result = Stream.of("banana", "kiwi", "apple", "fig")
    .filter(s -> s.length() > 3)     // banana, apple  (kiwi=4? no: 4>3 keeps kiwi too)
    .map(String::toUpperCase)         // transform survivors
    .sorted()                         // alphabetical
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
// trace: filter keeps banana(6), kiwi(4), apple(5) — fig(3) dropped
// map → BANANA, KIWI, APPLE;  sorted → [APPLE, BANANA, KIWI]
Intermediate ops (filter, map, sorted, distinct, limit) each return a NEW stream and do nothing until a terminal op runs — they’re lazy. Read a chain top-down and track the element list after every stage, exactly like the trace above.
⚠️ NO TERMINAL, NO WORK
A chain ending at .map(...) with no collect/forEach/count literally never executes — laziness is a graded fact. And streams are single-use: consuming one twice throws IllegalStateException.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Intermediate operations shape what flows through the pipeline. Knowing the dozen most useful ones — and their performance implications — lets you write expressive, fast streams. Misusing them turns elegant code into something that looks clever but runs slow.

Core concepts

1. filter(Predicate). Keeps only elements matching the predicate. .filter(s -> s.length() > 5). Stateless and cheap. Place filters as early in the pipeline as possible to reduce downstream work.

2. map(Function). Transforms each element. .map(String::toUpperCase). One-to-one mapping. mapToInt, mapToLong, mapToDouble produce primitive streams (faster, no boxing).

3. flatMap(Function). One-to-many mapping. .flatMap(list -> list.stream()) flattens nested collections. Essential for pipelines that produce streams from each element. Conceptually: map then concat.

4. distinct(). Removes duplicates using equals(). Stateful — must remember what it has seen. On large streams, can be expensive in memory. Consider HashSet-backed pre-deduplication if order doesn't matter.

5. sorted() and sorted(Comparator). Natural order or custom Comparator. Stateful — must collect and sort. On infinite streams, sorted will never terminate without an upstream limit.

6. limit(n) and skip(n). First n / drop first n. limit short-circuits, useful with infinite streams. skip is stateful. Both run in encounter order.

7. peek(Consumer). Performs a side effect without changing the stream. Almost always used for debugging — log each element flowing through. Avoid in production logic; if you need a side effect, you usually want forEach (a terminal).

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • filter AFTER map — works but transforms elements you'll discard. Filter first when possible.
  • Using peek for production logic — its execution order with parallel streams is unpredictable.
  • Boxing primitives unnecessarily — use mapToInt early to switch to IntStream when you can.
  • Stateful operations (sorted, distinct) on infinite streams without an upstream limit — runs forever.

Quick recap

filter and map are the workhorses; flatMap handles one-to-many shapes; distinct, sorted, limit, skip handle ordering and dedup. peek is a debugging tool. Place filters early and switch to primitive streams when you can to keep pipelines fast.

Glossary

Intermediate operation
A stream operation returning another stream; lazy.
Stateful operation
Operation requiring memory of previous elements (sorted, distinct, limit).
Stateless operation
Operation processing each element independently (map, filter).
IntStream / LongStream / DoubleStream
Primitive specializations avoiding boxing.
Short-circuit
Operation that may stop processing early once its result is determined (limit, findFirst).

Purity pays: a pure map function — no side effects, same input always yielding the same output — is predictable and PARALLEL-SAFE. That is what lets .parallelStream() work without race conditions.

📊 FIGURE — the two Java 9 short-circuiting slicers
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — takeWhile and dropWhile against filter, on the same data
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

List<Integer> nums = List.of(2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10);

System.out.println("takeWhile even: " +
    nums.stream().takeWhile(n -> n % 2 == 0).collect(Collectors.toList()));
System.out.println("dropWhile even: " +
    nums.stream().dropWhile(n -> n % 2 == 0).collect(Collectors.toList()));
System.out.println("filter even   : " +
    nums.stream().filter(n -> n % 2 == 0).collect(Collectors.toList()));
takeWhile even: [2, 4, 6] dropWhile even: [7, 8, 10] filter even : [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. takeWhile stops at the first element that fails the test — the 7 — and never looks further.
  2. dropWhile throws away exactly that leading run and keeps everything from the 7 onward, including the later even numbers.
  3. filter is the one that keeps every even number wherever it sits. That is the whole distinction: the first two care about position, filter cares only about the predicate.
🎯 EXAM TIP
A question that shows a list whose matching elements are interrupted — like 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10 — is testing exactly this. takeWhile gives [2, 4, 6], dropWhile gives [7, 8, 10], and only filter gives [2, 4, 6, 8, 10].

📖 Worked example — terminal operations & Collectors

WORKED EXAMPLE — the terminals you’ll actually use
List<Integer> nums = List.of(4, 1, 9, 4);

nums.stream().count();                          // 4
nums.stream().anyMatch(n -> n > 8);             // true
nums.stream().reduce(0, Integer::sum);          // 18  (fold it up)
nums.stream().distinct().collect(Collectors.toList());  // [4, 1, 9]
nums.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(n -> n % 2 == 0));
// {false=[1, 9], true=[4, 4]}   ← Map keyed by the classifier
Terminals END the stream and produce a value/side effect. reduce folds everything into one value with a starting identity; groupingBy is the workhorse collector — classifier function in, Map of lists out.
⚠️ collect vs reduce
Both terminate, but collect builds CONTAINERS (lists, maps, joined strings) and reduce folds to a SINGLE value. “Which produces a Map of employees by department?” → collect(groupingBy(...)), every time.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Terminal operations are where a stream pipeline produces something. collect() with a Collector is the most powerful — it reduces a stream to a List, Map, set of grouped values, or anything else. Mastering Collectors converts streams from a pretty syntax into a structural data-shaping tool.

Core concepts

1. The terminal categories. Reducing — sum, count, min, max, reduce. Collecting — collect into List, Set, Map. Iterating — forEach, forEachOrdered. Searching — findFirst, findAny, anyMatch, allMatch, noneMatch. Each terminal triggers the pipeline and produces a result.

2. collect(Collector). The most flexible terminal. A Collector specifies how to accumulate elements. The Collectors utility class provides ready-made collectors: toList, toSet, toMap, joining, groupingBy, partitioningBy, counting, summingInt, averagingDouble.

3. Collectors.toList() and toSet(). The bread and butter. stream.collect(Collectors.toList()) — modifiable List. stream.toList() (Java 16+) — unmodifiable List, slightly faster. Prefer toList() in modern code unless you need to mutate.

4. Collectors.toMap(keyFn, valueFn). Build a Map from a stream. Throws on duplicate keys; provide a merge function to handle duplicates. Common pitfall: forgetting the merge function and crashing on real-world data with duplicates.

5. groupingBy(classifier). Multi-map style: groups elements by classifier function into Map<K, List<V. Add a downstream collector for richer groupings — groupingBy(Person::city, counting()) gives count per city.

6. partitioningBy(predicate). Splits stream into Map<Boolean, List<T with true and false keys. Faster than groupingBy when you only have two groups.

7. reduce — when collectors aren't enough. stream.reduce(identity, accumulator) folds elements into a single value. For sums, use sum() or summingInt; for general aggregation, reduce. Most use cases are better served by a built-in collector.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • toMap without a merge function on data with duplicate keys — IllegalStateException at runtime.
  • Mixing Collectors.toList() (modifiable) with stream.toList() (unmodifiable) — UnsupportedOperationException on mutate.
  • forEach in parallel streams expecting order — use forEachOrdered or don't parallelize.
  • Using reduce when groupingBy or summingInt would express intent better.

Quick recap

Terminals trigger the pipeline. collect is the most flexible — combined with Collectors utilities, it shapes streams into Lists, Sets, Maps, grouped multimaps, partitioned splits, joined strings. Use ready-made collectors before reaching for raw reduce.

Glossary

Terminal operation
Triggers stream execution; produces a result or side effect.
Collector
Specification of how to accumulate stream elements into a result.
Collectors.toList()
Most common collector; gathers elements into a List.
groupingBy
Collector building Map<K, List<V by a classifier function.
reduce
General fold operation combining elements via an accumulator.

Collector fluency: Collectors.groupingBy(Order::getStatus) yields a Map from each status to the LIST of orders having it. Collectors.summarizingInt returns an IntSummaryStatistics carrying count, sum, min, average, and max — five aggregates in one pass.

📖 Worked example — when parallelStream() helps (and when it bites)

WORKED EXAMPLE — safe parallel sum vs unsafe shared state
// SAFE: no shared mutable state — combiner logic handles merging
long sum = numbers.parallelStream()
                  .mapToLong(n -> heavyCompute(n))
                  .sum();

// UNSAFE: many threads mutating one list — lost/corrupt elements
List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
numbers.parallelStream().forEach(out::add);      // DON'T
// fix: .collect(Collectors.toList())            // thread-safe by design
Parallel streams split the work across cores — a win for LARGE data with CPU-heavy, independent element work. The rule: no touching shared mutable variables inside the pipeline; let collectors do the merging.
⚠️ PARALLEL ISN’T FREE
Splitting/merging has overhead: small lists or cheap operations often run SLOWER in parallel. And ordering costs extra (forEachOrdered). Default to sequential; measure before parallelizing — that’s the expected exam judgment.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Parallel streams promise easy speedups: change .stream() to .parallelStream() and your code runs on multiple cores. But they have non-obvious requirements and costs. Used right, they save real time. Used wrong, they slow code down or break it subtly.

Core concepts

1. What parallel streams do. They split the source into chunks, process each chunk on a different thread (default: ForkJoinPool.commonPool), then combine results. The framework handles the splitting, dispatching, and merging.

2. When parallelism helps. Large data sets (thousands of elements minimum), CPU-bound work per element, stateless operations, side-effect-free pipelines. Image processing, large math computations, parsing thousands of records — these benefit.

3. When parallelism hurts. Small data sets — overhead dominates. I/O-bound work — thread context switches don't speed up waits. Order-dependent operations — parallel destroys order without forEachOrdered. Shared mutable state — race conditions.

4. The common pool. Parallel streams use ForkJoinPool.commonPool() by default. This pool is shared application-wide. Long-running parallel-stream tasks starve everything else using the pool. For dedicated parallelism, run inside your own ForkJoinPool.submit().

5. Side effects break parallelism. stream.parallel().forEach(list::add) — race condition on the list. Use thread-safe accumulation (Collectors.toList, ConcurrentHashMap) or a proper reduce. Side effects are the most common parallel-stream bug source.

6. forEach vs forEachOrdered. Parallel forEach runs in any order. forEachOrdered preserves encounter order at the cost of synchronization. If order matters in your terminal, you need forEachOrdered — or don't parallelize.

7. Measure, don't guess. Parallel speedup depends on data size, work per element, and hardware. Always benchmark with realistic data. The rule of thumb 'parallelize if work × elements > 10,000 simple ops' is a starting point, not a guarantee.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Parallelizing small streams — the parallelism overhead exceeds the work.
  • Side effects in parallel pipelines — data races, undefined behavior, occasional incorrect results.
  • Long-running parallel tasks blocking the common pool — system-wide slowdowns.
  • Assuming parallel will be faster without measuring — often it isn't.

Quick recap

Parallel streams split work across cores via ForkJoinPool. They help for large CPU-bound, stateless workloads with thread-safe accumulation. They hurt for small data, I/O-bound work, ordered output, or mutable shared state. Always measure; never assume.

Glossary

Parallel stream
A stream whose pipeline runs on multiple threads concurrently.
ForkJoinPool
Thread pool optimized for divide-and-conquer parallelism; backs parallel streams.
Common pool
Default ForkJoinPool shared by all parallel streams in the JVM.
Thread-safe accumulator
A Collector or accumulation strategy safe for concurrent updates.
forEachOrdered
Terminal preserving encounter order even in parallel.
"},"D387/ch3/s1":{"body":"

📖 Worked example — writing a generic class and method

WORKED EXAMPLE — one Box, every type
public class Box<T> {
    private T item;
    public void put(T item) { this.item = item; }
    public T get() { return item; }
}
Box<String> b = new Box<>();
b.put("hi");
String s = b.get();          // no cast — compiler knows it's String

// generic METHOD — the <T> before the return type declares it
public static <T> T firstOf(List<T> list) { return list.get(0); }
Integer n = firstOf(List.of(1, 2, 3));   // T inferred as Integer
T is a type parameter filled in at use. One implementation, compile-time safety for every instantiation — that’s the entire pitch of generics.
⚠️ ERASURE — GENERICS VANISH AT RUNTIME
At runtime Box<String> and Box<Integer> are the same class (type erasure): no T.class, no new T(), and instanceof Box<String> won’t compile. Generics are a COMPILE-TIME contract.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Generics give you compile-time type safety without runtime overhead. They let one List<String reject Integers without runtime casts, and they let you write a single sort method that handles any comparable type. Without generics, Java code is full of unsafe casts and ClassCastExceptions.

Core concepts

1. Generic class declaration. class Box<T { T value; T get() { return value; } void set(T v) { value = v; } }. The <T after the class name introduces a type parameter. T is a placeholder filled when the class is used: Box<String, Box<Integer.

2. Multiple type parameters. Map<K, V has two: key and value. Pair<L, R. Convention: T (type), E (element), K (key), V (value), R (return). One letter unless naming clarifies.

3. Generic methods. <T List<T singletonList(T item). The <T before the return type makes the method generic, independent of the class. The compiler infers T from arguments.

4. Type erasure. At runtime, generic type information is erased. Box<String and Box<Integer are both just Box. This preserves backward compatibility but means you cannot ask 'is this a List<String?' at runtime — only 'is this a List?'

5. Cannot instantiate type parameters. new T() is forbidden — at runtime T doesn't exist. Workaround: take a Class<T parameter and use clazz.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance(), or take a Supplier<T.

6. Cannot create generic arrays. new T[10] is forbidden. new List<String[10] is forbidden. The reasons trace to type erasure plus array runtime type checks. Use ArrayList<List<String or Object[] with casts (with caution).

7. Generics and inheritance. List<Dog is NOT a subtype of List<Animal, even though Dog is a subtype of Animal. This invariance prevents runtime errors when you try to add a Cat to a 'List<Animal' that's actually a List<Dog. Wildcards (next section) recover the flexibility safely.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Using raw types (List instead of List<String) — defeats type safety, generates compiler warnings.
  • Trying new T() or new T[10] — won't compile; redesign with Class<T, Supplier<T, or ArrayList.
  • Assuming List<Dog is a List<Animal — invariance is your friend, not an annoyance.
  • Adding @SuppressWarnings to silence generic warnings without understanding why — usually masks a real type bug.

Quick recap

Generics make collections and APIs type-safe at compile time. Class-level type parameters parameterize the class; method-level parameterize a single method. Type erasure means generics are a compile-time fiction at runtime. Generics are invariant — wildcards recover variance safely (next section).

Glossary

Type parameter
A placeholder type (T, E, K, V) introduced in <> on a class or method.
Generic class
Class parameterized by one or more type parameters.
Generic method
Method introducing its own type parameter, independent of any class parameter.
Type erasure
Runtime removal of generic type info; preserves backward compatibility.
Invariance
List<Dog is NOT a List<Animal, even though Dog is an Animal.

📖 Worked example — bounds & wildcards (PECS)

WORKED EXAMPLE — Producer Extends, Consumer Super
// ? extends Number → a PRODUCER you read from
double total(List<? extends Number> src) {
    double t = 0;
    for (Number n : src) t += n.doubleValue();   // reading OK
    // src.add(1);  ← forbidden: exact type unknown
    return t;
}
total(List.of(1, 2));        // List<Integer> accepted
total(List.of(1.5, 2.5));    // List<Double> accepted

// ? super Integer → a CONSUMER you write into
void fill(List<? super Integer> dst) { dst.add(42); }   // writing OK
PECS: Producer → extends (safe to READ as the bound); Consumer → super (safe to WRITE the bound in). A bounded type parameter <T extends Comparable<T>> similarly promises “T can compare itself,” unlocking sort/max.
⚠️ CAN’T ADD TO ? extends
Into a List<? extends Number> you may add NOTHING (except null) — it might really be a List<Integer> and you might be holding a Double. Read-only-ness of extends is the most-tested consequence.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Plain generics are invariant — too restrictive in practice. Bounded type parameters and wildcards add controlled variance: 'any subtype of Number' or 'any supertype of String.' These are how production APIs like Collections.sort, Stream.map, and the Comparable interface stay flexible without sacrificing safety.

Core concepts

1. Upper-bounded type parameter. <T extends Number — T is some subtype of Number. The method can call Number's methods on T. Useful when the algorithm needs capabilities the bound provides. Example: <T extends Comparable<T T max(List<T list).

2. Multiple bounds. <T extends Number & Comparable<T. T is both. The class bound (if any) must come first; the rest are interfaces. Used when you need capabilities from multiple types.

3. Wildcard introduction. List means 'a list of some unknown type.' You can read from it (as Object) but not add anything except null. Used when you want to accept lists of varying element types without caring which.

4. Upper-bounded wildcard . 'A list of T or any subtype.' List can accept List<Integer, List<Double. You can read elements as Number; you cannot add (because the actual type is unknown — adding a Number to a List<Integer would break it). This is the PRODUCER pattern.

5. Lower-bounded wildcard . 'A list of T or any supertype.' List can accept List<Number, List<Object. You can add Integer (any supertype list accepts an Integer); you cannot read meaningfully (only as Object). This is the CONSUMER pattern.

6. PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. The mnemonic for which wildcard to use. If the parameter PRODUCES values for your code (you read from it), use ? extends T. If it CONSUMES values from your code (you write to it), use ? super T. Think Collections.copy(dest, src): src is a producer (extends T), dest is a consumer (super T).

7. Where bounds and wildcards differ. Use bounded type parameter <T extends X when you need to refer to T multiple times or return it. Use bounded wildcard when you don't need to name the type — typically a parameter, used once, no return.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Trying to add elements to a List — compile error; that's the point.
  • Using <T extends X when would be sufficient — adds unnecessary type-parameter noise.
  • Forgetting PECS and writing methods that look 'flexible' but actually exclude valid callers.
  • Confusing T extends X (type parameter) with ? extends X (wildcard) — they look similar but have different rules.

Quick recap

Bounds add capabilities to type parameters; wildcards add variance. <T extends X when you need to name the type; when reading; when writing. PECS — Producer Extends, Consumer Super — captures the choice in four words.

Glossary

Bounded type parameter
<T extends X — T must be a subtype of X.
Upper-bounded wildcard
— unknown type that is a subtype of X; producer.
Lower-bounded wildcard
— unknown type that is a supertype of X; consumer.
Unbounded wildcard
— unknown type; can only read as Object, can add only null.
PECS
Producer Extends, Consumer Super — wildcard selection mnemonic.

📖 Worked example — picking the right collection

WORKED EXAMPLE — requirements → implementation
• “Fast index access, mostly reads” → ArrayList (O(1) get).
• “No duplicates, order irrelevant, fast contains” → HashSet (O(1) average).
• “No duplicates, iterate in sorted order” → TreeSet (O(log n), sorted).
• “Key → value lookup” → HashMap; need sorted keys → TreeMap; need insertion order preserved → LinkedHashMap.
• “FIFO processing” → ArrayDeque as a queue.

Map<String,Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();
for (String w : words)
    counts.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum);   // count occurrences in one line
⚠️ HASH COLLECTIONS NEED THE CONTRACT
HashSet/HashMap only behave if elements/keys implement equals() AND hashCode() consistently. A custom key class missing hashCode → “contains says false for an equal object” — the bug and the exam question are the same sentence.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The Java collections framework is a finely-tuned library, but most developers use 5% of it well and the rest by guess. Knowing which collection has which performance profile and what newer additions like Map.of and List.copyOf give you is the difference between code that runs and code that scales.

Core concepts

1. The interface hierarchy. Collection at the top. List (ordered, indexed), Set (unique), Queue (FIFO), Deque (double-ended). Map is separate (key-value). Each interface has multiple concrete implementations with different performance characteristics.

2. List implementations. ArrayList — array-backed, O(1) random access, O(n) insertion at front. LinkedList — node-based, O(1) front/back insert, O(n) random access. ArrayList wins almost always; LinkedList only when you frequently insert/remove at front and never random-access.

3. Set implementations. HashSet — O(1) add/contains, no order. LinkedHashSet — same plus insertion order. TreeSet — sorted, O(log n). Pick by need: hash for speed, linked for predictable order, tree for sorted iteration.

4. Map implementations. HashMap — O(1) put/get, no order. LinkedHashMap — insertion (or access) order. TreeMap — sorted by key, O(log n). EnumMap — for enum keys, very fast and compact. ConcurrentHashMap — thread-safe HashMap.

5. Queue and Deque. ArrayDeque is the modern fast deque (faster than LinkedList for queue/stack uses). PriorityQueue for ordered retrieval (heap-based). For producer-consumer concurrency, use BlockingQueue implementations.

6. Immutable factories (Java 9+). List.of(a, b, c), Set.of(a, b, c), Map.of(k1, v1, k2, v2). Compact, type-inferred, immutable. Mutation throws UnsupportedOperationException. Use them for constants and read-only data; reach for ArrayList only when mutation is needed.

7. Collections utility class. Collections.sort, Collections.unmodifiableList, Collections.synchronizedList, Collections.frequency, Collections.binarySearch. The 'static helpers' for collections. Many uses superseded by Stream API or modern factories, but Collections.unmodifiableList still has its place when wrapping a mutable list.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Defaulting to LinkedList when ArrayList wins on almost every workload.
  • Using HashMap when iteration order matters — switch to LinkedHashMap.
  • Forgetting that Map.of() throws on duplicate keys (unlike Map.put which overwrites).
  • Sharing a non-thread-safe collection across threads without synchronization or copying.

Quick recap

ArrayList for lists, HashMap for maps, HashSet for sets — defaults that win 80% of the time. Reach for LinkedHashMap, TreeMap, ArrayDeque, EnumMap when their specific properties match the need. Use Map.of, List.of, Set.of for immutable constants. Collections is the older utility class; many of its features are now in Stream API.

Glossary

ArrayList
Array-backed List; O(1) get, O(n) middle insert.
LinkedList
Doubly-linked List; O(1) front/back insert, O(n) get.
HashMap
Hash-based Map; O(1) average put/get; unordered.
TreeMap
Sorted Map (Red-Black tree); O(log n).
List.of / Map.of
Java 9+ immutable factory methods producing compact unmodifiable collections.

Iterable vs Iterator: an Iterable is something that CAN be iterated — it has an iterator() method. An Iterator is the actual CURSOR doing the walking — hasNext() and next(). Collections are Iterable; each loop gets its own Iterator.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Threads are the foundation of Java concurrency. Even when you use Executors and CompletableFuture, you are building on threads. Understanding what a thread actually is, how to start one, and the lifecycle states it moves through is the bedrock that everything else rests on.

Core concepts

1. What a thread is. An independent path of execution within a process. Each thread has its own stack but shares the heap with other threads in the same process. The OS schedules threads onto CPU cores.

2. Two ways to define a thread's work. Implement Runnable (preferred) — class implements Runnable, override run(). Pass to new Thread(runnable). Or extend Thread directly (less flexible — Java has single inheritance, so extending Thread blocks extending anything else).

3. Starting a thread. thread.start() — schedules for execution; the JVM eventually calls run() on the new thread. NEVER call thread.run() directly — that runs the code on the current thread. The most common rookie mistake.

4. Thread states. NEW (created, not started), RUNNABLE (running or ready to run), BLOCKED (waiting for monitor lock), WAITING (Object.wait, Thread.join with no timeout), TIMED_WAITING (sleep, wait with timeout), TERMINATED (run returned). Thread.getState() returns the current state.

5. join, sleep, interrupt. join() — wait for the thread to finish. sleep(ms) — pause the current thread (NOT the target). interrupt() — set the thread's interrupted flag; cooperative shutdown signal. Properly handling interruption is part of writing well-behaved concurrent code.

6. Daemon threads. Daemon threads die when the JVM exits — they don't keep the JVM alive. setDaemon(true) BEFORE start. Useful for background utilities (timers, GC helpers). Default is non-daemon (user thread).

7. Why raw threads are rarely the right choice. Creating a thread costs ~1MB of stack space and OS resources. Spawning a thread per task scales badly. Use Executors (later in this chapter) to pool threads and queue work. Direct Thread is for rare special cases.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Calling thread.run() instead of thread.start() — runs synchronously on the current thread.
  • Spawning thousands of raw threads — memory exhaustion and scheduling overhead. Use Executors.
  • Ignoring InterruptedException — silently swallowing it breaks cooperative cancellation.
  • Setting daemon AFTER start — IllegalThreadStateException.

Quick recap

A thread is an independent execution path. Define work with Runnable; create with new Thread(runnable); start with start() (never run()). Threads move through NEW → RUNNABLE → ... → TERMINATED. Daemon threads don't keep the JVM alive. Prefer Executors over raw threads in production code.

Glossary

Thread
An independent path of execution within a process.
Runnable
Functional interface representing work to run on a thread.
start() vs run()
start() launches the thread; run() executes synchronously on the current thread.
Daemon thread
Thread that does not keep the JVM alive.
InterruptedException
Checked exception signaling cooperative cancellation.

📖 Worked example — a race condition, then the fix

WORKED EXAMPLE — count++ across two threads
class Counter {
    private int count = 0;
    void increment() { count++; }        // read + add + write: 3 steps!
}
// Two threads, 1000 increments each → final count often < 2000:
// both read 500, both write 501 — one update LOST.

class SafeCounter {
    private int count = 0;
    synchronized void increment() { count++; }   // one thread at a time
}
// or: AtomicInteger count; count.incrementAndGet();
count++ isn’t atomic, so concurrent updates interleave and vanish. synchronized puts a lock around the method (mutual exclusion); AtomicInteger does it lock-free. Both end at exactly 2000.
⚠️ SYNCHRONIZE THE SMALLEST THING THAT WORKS
Locks serialize — too much synchronized and threads queue up (or deadlock if two locks are taken in opposite orders). Guard the shared mutable state, not entire workflows; prefer atomics/concurrent collections when they fit.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

When threads share mutable state, race conditions and visibility bugs lurk. Synchronization gives you mutual exclusion and memory visibility. Locks give you finer control. Understanding both — and the volatile keyword — is the difference between correct concurrent code and code that 'works on my machine.'

Core concepts

1. Race conditions and atomicity. When two threads modify shared state without coordination, the result depends on interleaving. counter++ is three operations (read, add, write); two threads can both read 5 and both write 6, losing an increment. Operations that must be atomic need explicit synchronization.

2. The synchronized keyword. synchronized methods or blocks acquire a monitor lock before executing and release on exit. Only one thread holds a given lock at a time. synchronized (this) — instance lock. synchronized (SomeClass.class) — class lock. The simplest correctness primitive.

3. Memory visibility — the volatile keyword. Without volatile, a write in one thread may not be visible to reads in another thread for an unbounded time (CPU caches, JIT optimizations). volatile guarantees writes flush to main memory and reads see the latest value. Lighter than synchronized but only for single-variable writes/reads.

4. The Lock interface (java.util.concurrent.locks). ReentrantLock is the modern alternative to synchronized. tryLock() — non-blocking attempt. lockInterruptibly() — responds to interrupt. fairness option — FIFO ordering. Required idiom: try { lock.lock(); ... } finally { lock.unlock(); } — the finally is mandatory.

5. ReadWriteLock. Readers don't block readers; writers block everyone. ReentrantReadWriteLock for cases with many reads and few writes. Caveat: not always faster than a plain lock; benchmark before assuming.

6. StampedLock (Java 8+). Optimistic read mode for hot read paths. Faster than ReadWriteLock for read-heavy workloads. More complex API; use when you've measured and need it.

7. Atomic classes are usually better. AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, AtomicReference — single-variable atomicity without explicit locks. AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() is atomic and faster than synchronized for single-counter use cases. Reach for atomics first; reach for locks when atomics aren't enough.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Forgetting to release a lock in finally — deadlock when an exception is thrown.
  • Using synchronized to protect long-running operations — blocks other threads unnecessarily; release the lock and re-acquire in a loop instead.
  • Assuming volatile makes compound operations atomic — counter++ is still racy even with volatile.
  • Mixing synchronized blocks and Lock objects on the same data — guaranteed bugs.

Quick recap

Race conditions need either atomic operations or mutual exclusion. synchronized is the simplest tool. volatile gives visibility but not atomicity. ReentrantLock adds tryLock and interruptibility. ReadWriteLock helps read-heavy workloads. Atomic classes solve single-variable updates without locks.

Glossary

Race condition
Outcome depends on the unpredictable interleaving of threads.
synchronized
Java keyword providing mutual exclusion via monitor locks.
volatile
Keyword guaranteeing memory visibility for a single variable; not atomicity for compound ops.
ReentrantLock
Explicit lock with tryLock, fairness, and interruptibility options.
AtomicInteger
Lock-free atomic integer with operations like incrementAndGet.
📊 FIGURE — two waits that look alike and are not
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A latch: one thread waits for three workers to finish
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

CountDownLatch latch = new CountDownLatch(3);
AtomicInteger finished = new AtomicInteger();

for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    new Thread(() -> {
        finished.incrementAndGet();
        latch.countDown();
    }).start();
}

latch.await();
System.out.println("workers finished: " + finished.get());
System.out.println("latch count now : " + latch.getCount());
latch.countDown();
System.out.println("after another countDown: " + latch.getCount());
workers finished: 3 latch count now : 0 after another countDown: 0
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. await() blocks the main thread until the count reaches 0 — that is what makes the printed total reliably 3 rather than whatever happened to be done.
  2. The count only ever goes down. Once it is 0, further countDown() calls do nothing, which is why the last line still prints 0.
  3. That one-way behaviour is the point: a latch marks something that happens once, such as "startup finished" or "all workers done".
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A barrier: the same three threads meeting twice
import java.util.concurrent.CyclicBarrier;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

AtomicInteger phase = new AtomicInteger();
CyclicBarrier barrier = new CyclicBarrier(3,
    () -> System.out.println("phase " + phase.incrementAndGet() + " complete"));

Thread[] ts = new Thread[3];
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    ts[i] = new Thread(() -> {
        try {
            barrier.await();   // phase 1
            barrier.await();   // phase 2
        } catch (Exception e) { }
    });
    ts[i].start();
}
for (Thread t : ts) t.join();
System.out.println("parties: " + barrier.getParties() + ", reusable: true");
phase 1 complete phase 2 complete parties: 3, reusable: true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The barrier action runs once per phase, on whichever thread arrives last — so "phase 1 complete" prints only after all three have arrived.
  2. The same barrier then re-arms automatically, which is why the second await() works and phase 2 completes too.
  3. A CountDownLatch could not do this: it would be spent after the first round.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Choosing a latch when the threads must meet repeatedly. A CountDownLatch cannot be reset, so a second round waits forever. The rule of thumb: latch = wait for events, once; barrier = wait for each other, repeatedly.
